unit.name: Deconvolution foundations: upsampling and transposed convolution
unit.description: Motivates deconvolution from GANs and segmentation, then derives a 1D convolution as matrix multiplication to explain why deconvolution is commonly implemented as transposed convolution.
unit.summary: The final CNN method begins by motivating deconvolution through generative models and dense prediction: generators need to grow a low-dimensional code into an image, and segmentation networks downsample then upsample so each pixel receives a class [ts=2935s] [ts=3007s]. The instructor states that this matters for interpretability because a deconvolutional module can reverse-engineer the trace of a high activation back toward the input [ts=3051s]. A 1D convolution with padding, filter size, and stride is rewritten as a matrix-vector multiplication y = Wx [ts=3096s] [ts=3273s]. From that view, deconvolution is approximated in practice as a transposed convolution, with the implementation intuition of inserting zeros/sub-pixels, flipping filters, and reducing stride [ts=3351s] [ts=3513s].

key_points.text: GAN generators use deconvolution or upsampling to turn a random code into an image-shaped output.
Segmentation architectures downsample with convolutions and then upsample so the output has per-pixel predictions.
A deconvolutional module can be used to reverse-engineer why a specific activation was high.
A 1D convolution can be written as a matrix-vector product y = Wx.
Deconvolution is treated as a transposed convolution when the inverse is approximated by W transpose.
A sub-pixel deconvolution implementation inserts zeros/padding, flips the filters, and divides the stride.
